title: The football field and the hard cases

blocks.md:
Every method in this chapter produces a different answer for the same company. That is not a failure of the methods — it is the point, and the last thing a candidate learns is how to say so out loud.

Two questions come out of it. "How would you present a valuation to a client?" tests whether you understand that bankers deliver ranges, not numbers. "How would you value a company with negative cash flows?" tests whether your toolkit collapses the moment the company stops looking like a textbook.

Both are asked at summer level, and the second one catches people who have only ever practised on profitable companies.

blocks.heading: The gaps between the methods are the analysis
blocks.md:
A **football field** is the chart bankers actually put in front of a board: one horizontal bar per method, each bar spanning the range that reasonable assumptions produce, with the current share price and the 52-week trading range drawn across as reference lines.

Read it in two passes.

The **overlap** — the vertical band where several bars agree — is the range you can defend under questioning. If comps and precedents both support £12 to £13, that band survives contact with a sceptical client.

The **gaps** are where the thinking lives. Precedents sitting above comps is not noise; it is the price of control, quantified. A DCF sitting below the market price is not an error; it is a statement that your projections are more conservative than the market's, and you should be able to say which assumption is doing it.

That is why the chart has bars rather than a single number. The moment you average them, you have deleted the only interesting information on the page.

**Building one, in order.** Run each method, convert every output to a **per-share** figure so the bars are comparable, then draw them against the market.

Converting is the step people fumble under pressure. Trading and deal multiples give you an *enterprise value*, so each one has to come back across the bridge before it can sit next to a share price:

$$\text{Per share} = \frac{\text{Implied EV} - \text{debt} - \text{leases} + \text{cash}}{\text{diluted shares}}$$

For Marlow that means deducting £210m — £240m of borrowings plus £30m of leases, less £60m of cash — and dividing by 120m shares, every single time.

**When the company has no earnings**, the structure of the chart survives but its contents change:

- Trading and deal multiples move down the income statement to **revenue**, or to a sector measure — subscribers, recurring revenue, reserves, beds.
- The **DCF runs longer**, with an explicit period stretching to whenever profitability arrives rather than the usual five years.
- The bars get **wider**, and you say so rather than hiding it.

A wide range honestly drawn is worth more than a narrow one you cannot defend.

blocks.prompt: Your DCF values Marlow at £9.50 a share. Precedent transactions imply £13.88. A client asks: "So what is it actually worth?" What is the best response?

options.label: "It depends who is buying: £8.67–£10.33 as a standalone business, £12–£14 to an acquirer taking control."
"£13.88 — it is the highest number we can defend."
"We would need to rerun the DCF until it agrees with the precedents."

blocks.explain_md:
The two numbers are not competing estimates of one truth — they answer **different questions**. The DCF says what the business is worth run as it is today. The precedents say what someone has paid for the right to control a similar business and change it.

So the honest answer names both and attaches each to a buyer. Averaging them produces a number that describes nobody's situation; picking the highest is advocacy, not analysis. This is also the shape of the answer when an interviewer pushes you for "one number" — give the range, then say what would move you within it.

blocks.md:
**Marlow's football field, built from the chapter's own numbers.** EBITDA is £150m, the bridge deduction is £210m and there are 120m shares.

The peer set runs from 8.0× to 12.0× EV/EBITDA with a median of 11.0×; the four precedent deals run 11.0× to 14.0× with a median of 12.5×; the DCF chapter produces an enterprise value of £1,250–1,450m. Convert each to a per-share figure and the chart draws itself.

steps.label: Comps at the median 11.0× — implied EV

blocks.md: Finish the chart. The DCF gives an enterprise value between £1,250m and £1,450m; the precedent set reaches 14.0× at the top. Then find the band where the two market-based methods actually agree — the number you would defend to a board.

steps.label: Width of the overlap: comps high less precedents low

blocks.md:
**"Take the average of the three methods."**

It sounds even-handed and it destroys the analysis. Averaging asserts that the three methods are three noisy attempts at one number, when they are answers to three different questions — what the market pays for businesses like this one, what an acquirer pays for control of one, and what the cash flows are worth on your own assumptions.

Marlow makes the cost visible. Averaging the midpoints of £12.00, £13.88 and £9.50 gives about £11.79 — a figure no method supports, sitting in a gap between two of the bars, and impossible to defend when a client asks where it came from.

Worse, it throws away the two most interesting facts on the chart: that precedents sit roughly 30 % above the undisturbed price, which is the control premium made concrete, and that the DCF lands below the market, which is your projections telling you something. Both are conversations. The average is a full stop.

You present a football field: one horizontal bar per method, each showing the range that reasonable assumptions produce, with the current share price and 52-week range as reference lines. The overlap between methods is the defensible range; the gaps are what you explain. For a company with negative cash flows, the multiples move to revenue or an operating measure, the DCF runs a longer explicit period until profitability arrives, and you lean on the drivers that eventually produce cash — growth, gross margin and unit economics.

tmt.heading: Presenting a company that does not make money yet
tmt.md:
The football field for a loss-making software business looks the same and contains different bars. Trading comps become **EV/ARR** against listed peers; precedents become EV/ARR paid in recent software deals; and the DCF bar is far and away the widest on the page.

That width is not sloppiness. In a company whose profits arrive in year seven, almost all of the present value sits in the terminal assumption, so a plausible range of terminal margins produces a range of values that can be twice as wide at the top as at the bottom. Trying to narrow it by pretending to precision is worse than showing it.

One extra line is usually worth adding: **the last private funding round**. For a company that recently raised, that price is a real transaction in the actual asset, and boards ask about it whether or not you have drawn it.
tmt.example_q: How do you explain a DCF range on the football field that is twice as wide at the top as at the bottom?
tmt.answer_md:
I would say plainly that it reflects where the value sits. For a company that only becomes profitable late in the forecast, most of the present value is in the terminal year, so the range is really a range of terminal assumptions — the exit multiple or the steady-state margin — rather than a range of near-term trading.

Then I would show the sensitivity grid beside it, so the board can see which assumption is doing the work and form their own view rather than accepting mine. And I would anchor the discussion on the ARR multiples instead, because those are observable today.

The wide bar is honest. Narrowing it would mean pretending to know the terminal margin more precisely than anyone does.

healthcare.heading: One bar per programme
healthcare.md:
For a clinical-stage biotech the chart is not organised by method at all — it is organised **by asset**, because that is how the company is actually worth anything.

Each drug programme gets its own bar: a risk-adjusted NPV built from expected peak sales, the probability the drug reaches approval, and the timing of launch. Below them sit the balance-sheet items that are certain — net cash — and any platform or technology value that does not belong to a single programme. Add them up and you have a sum of the parts.

The cross-check comes from precedents: what acquirers have paid per unit of risk-adjusted peak sales for companies at a similar stage. If your rNPV implies a valuation far above recent deals for comparable assets, the probabilities are probably generous.

Because the outcomes are binary, boards usually want **scenario bars** alongside the expected case — what the company is worth if the readout succeeds, and what is left if it fails.
healthcare.example_q: How would a healthcare banker present a Phase 3 company to its board?
healthcare.answer_md:
As a sum of the parts, one bar per programme rather than one bar per method. Each programme would carry a risk-adjusted NPV with the probability of success stated explicitly on the page, because that assumption drives the answer more than anything else and the board should be arguing about it.

Underneath I would put net cash, which is certain, and any platform value separately so it is not smuggled into a drug's number.

Because a Phase 3 readout is close to binary, I would show scenario bars beside the expected case — the value on approval and the value on failure, which is often not far above the cash. Then I would cross-check the whole thing against precedent deals for similar-stage assets on a peak-sales basis, and flag any programme where my rNPV implies a price nobody has actually paid.

blocks.prompt: Marlow is considering buying a **pre-revenue diagnostics start-up**. It has no earnings and expects its first £5m of revenue in two years. List, in order, the methods you would use — and for each, the single number that matters most.
blocks.model_answer_md:
I would use four, and I would tell the client up front that the range will be wide.

**1. A DCF with a long explicit period.** Ten years rather than five, running to whenever the business is genuinely profitable. The number that matters is the **terminal margin** — what this business looks like at maturity — because with nothing in the early years, almost all the value sits at the end.

**2. EV/forward revenue against early-stage listed peers.** The number that matters is the **growth rate**, because that is what separates a company worth 3× forward revenue from one worth 12×.

**3. Precedent transactions in diagnostics.** The number that matters is the **EV/revenue multiple actually paid**, ideally for targets at a similar stage — this is the only evidence of what a real buyer has parted with.

**4. A venture-capital-style sanity check.** Work back from a plausible exit value at a required return. The number that matters is the **required return**, which for an asset this early is likely 30 % or more.

I would present these as a wide band and be explicit that the DCF bar is the widest, because for a company with no revenue the honest answer is a range with the assumptions on display — not a point estimate dressed up as precision.
rubric: Moves the multiples from earnings to revenue or a sector measure
Extends the DCF horizon beyond the usual five years and says why
Identifies one dominant driver per method rather than listing methods alone
States that the resulting range will be wide, and why that is the honest answer
Orders the methods sensibly rather than presenting them as interchangeable

pairs.a: A chart of per-share valuation ranges, one bar per method, with the market price and 52-week range as reference lines.

pairs.q: Negative EBITDA — which multiple do you reach for?
pairs.a: EV/Revenue, or a sector measure such as recurring revenue, subscribers or reserves.
It anchors the analysis to where the shares have actually traded, not just where the models say they should.

pairs.q: When is a DCF the only usable method?
pairs.a: When there are no listed peers and no recent deals — a unique asset, such as a single piece of infrastructure.

blocks.md: **The overlap between the methods is the answer you defend; the gaps between them are the analysis you explain — which is why you never take the average.**

items: I can describe a football field and say what each bar and reference line is for.
I can convert an implied enterprise value into a per-share figure without fumbling the bridge.
I can explain why averaging the methods destroys the information in the chart.
I can lay out a valuation approach for a company with no revenue and no earnings.
I can answer "so what is it worth?" with a range tied to who is buying.
